title: INT 15h, the BIOS system services
covers: INT 15h, the BIOS system services: the A20 gate calls, the configuration table and the Amstrad ROS version.

rows.text: INT 15h AH=06h gets the ROS version number of the Amstrad PC1512.
BX is the version number.
On an Amstrad machine the handler dispatches AH below 7 first, and reaches it by the case 0x06 of that dispatch.
The call also clears CF.
On an Amstrad machine the call also reaches the main dispatch, where case 0x06 only logs an unknown-function message.

closed.reason: cases of the other Amstrad calls, AH 0x00 to 0x05
default case of the Amstrad dispatch, for other AH values

ES:BX points to the ROM table (see #00509).

The PC XT (since 1986/01/10), PC AT (since 1985/06/10), PC XT Model 286, PC Convertible and most PS/2 machines clear CF and return the table in ES:BX.
AH 80h is an unsupported function: the PC and PCjr return AH=80h with CF set.

The configuration table is at F000h:E6F5h in 100% compatible BIOSes.
The INT 15h handler reaches it by the case 0xC0 of its main dispatch.

Whatever the machine type, the case itself stores ES as biosConfigSeg, BX as 0 and AH as 0x00, and clears CF.

rows.text: INT 15h AH=4Fh is the keyboard intercept, called by the INT 09h handler to translate scan codes.
AL is the hardware scan code on entry.
CF is set on entry.
CF set on return means continue processing the scan code.
AL is the possibly-altered hardware scan code.
CF clear on return means the scan code should be ignored.
The INT 09h code does not examine the scan code it reads from the keyboard until this function returns, so software can rearrange the keyboard.
Examples of rearranging: swapping the CapsLock and Control keys, or turning the right Shift key into Enter.
DOS 6 KEYB.COM does not pass through this function when Ctrl-Alt-Del is pressed and a SmartDrive v4-compatible cache with dirty buffers is installed.
IBM classifies this function as required.
The INT 15h handler reaches it by the case 0x4f of its main dispatch.
This case does not read AL.
This case does not read CF.
This case does not store AL, so the scan code is returned as it came in.
This case never clears CF: it sets CF on every call.
INT 15h AH=83h sets an event wait interval.
AL=00h sets the interval.
CX:DX is the number of microseconds to delay.
ES:BX points to a byte whose high bit is to be set at the end of the interval.
AL=01h cancels the wait interval.
CF is set on error.
CF is set if the function is already busy.
AH=80h means invalid command (PC, PCjr).
AH=86h means function not supported (XT and later).
CF is clear if successful.
The resolution of the wait period is 977 microseconds on many systems because many BIOSes use the 1/1024 second fast interrupt of the AT real-time clock.
The IBM AT BIOS dated 1984/1/10 ignores AL and always performs subfunction 00h.
The INT 15h handler reaches it by the case 0x83 of its main dispatch.
AL 0x01 cancels the wait; any other AL takes the set-interval path, unless a wait is already active.
AH 0x80 is stored when a wait is already active, and nowhere else in the case, so not for an invalid command.
This case never stores AH 0x86.
INT 15h AH=84h is joystick support, for the XT after 1982/11/8, the AT, XT286 and PS.
DX=0000h reads the joystick switches.
For DX=0000h, AL bits 7-4 are the switch settings.
DX=0001h reads the positions of the joysticks.
For DX=0001h, AX is the X position of joystick A.
For DX=0001h, BX is the Y position of joystick A.
For DX=0001h, CX is the X position of joystick B.
For DX=0001h, DX is the Y position of joystick B.
CF is set on error.
On error AH is the status (see #00496).
CF is clear if successful.
If no game port is installed, DX=0000h returns AL=00h (all switches open).
If no game port is installed, DX=0001h returns AX=BX=CX=DX=0000h.
A 250kOhm joystick typically returns 0000h-01A0h.
The INT 15h handler reaches it by the case 0x84 of its main dispatch.
A DX other than 0x0000 and 0x0001 only logs an error message and changes no register.
When only joystick B is enabled, AX and BX are stored 0 and CX and DX hold joystick B's positions.
For DX=0x0000 with neither joystick enabled, the case stores AX 0x00F0 and DX 0x0201 and sets CF, not AL 0x00.
CF is set when neither joystick is enabled; an unknown DX only logs an error and leaves CF alone.
This case has no store of a status in AH: AH changes only as the high byte of a whole-AX store.
INT 15h AH=86h waits, for the AT and PS.
CX:DX is the interval in microseconds.
CF is clear if successful, meaning the wait interval elapsed.
CF is set on error.
CF is set if an AH=83h wait is already in progress.
On error AH is the status (see #00496).
The resolution of the wait period is 977 microseconds on many systems because many BIOSes use the 1/1024 second fast interrupt of the AT real-time clock.
Newer BIOSes may have more precise timers, so the function cannot be used accurately for very short delays unless the BIOS's precise behavior is known.
The INT 15h handler reaches it by the case 0x86 of its main dispatch.
The wait flag pointer is set to segment 0 and the fixed offset BIOS_WAIT_FLAG_TEMP.
Without the unmask option the wait only logs an error when IRQ 2 or IRQ 8 is masked; with it, the wait loop logs a warning and unmasks them.
The wait is a loop that calls CALLBACK_Idle on each pass while the count stored at the wait flag is not 0.
INT 15h AH=87h copies extended memory.
CX is the number of words to copy.
The number of words in CX is at most 8000h.
ES:SI points to the global descriptor table (see #00499).
CF is set on error.
CF is clear if successful.
AH is the status (see #00498).
The default BIOS handler does the copy in protected mode with interrupts disabled.
Many 386 memory managers perform the copy with interrupts enabled.
This function is incompatible with the OS/2 compatibility box.
AH=00h means the source was copied into the destination.
AH=01h means parity error.
AH=02h means interrupt error.
AH=03h means address line 20 gating failed.
AH=80h means invalid command (PC, PCjr).
AH=86h means unsupported function (XT, PS30).
Offset 00h of the table is 16 bytes of zeros, used by the BIOS.
Offset 10h is a WORD, the source segment length in bytes (2*CX-1 or greater).
Offset 12h is 3 BYTEs, the 24-bit linear source address, low byte first.
Offset 15h is a BYTE, the source segment access rights (93h).
Offset 16h is a WORD: zero on a 286; on a 386+ the extended access rights and the high byte of the source address.
Offset 18h is a WORD, the destination segment length in bytes (2*CX-1 or greater).
Offset 1Ah is 3 BYTEs, the 24-bit linear destination address, low byte first.
Offset 1Dh is a BYTE, the destination segment access rights (93h).
Offset 1Eh is a WORD: zero on a 286; on a 386+ the extended access rights and the high byte of the destination address.
Offset 20h is 16 bytes of zeros, used by the BIOS to build the CS and SS descriptors.
The INT 15h handler reaches it by the case 0x87 of its main dispatch.
The case copies with MEM_BlockCopy on physical addresses, without entering protected mode; it enables A20 first and restores its previous state afterwards.
After the copy the case sets the segment limits of CS, DS, ES and SS to 0xFFFF.
This case does not compare CX with 0x8000 or limit it.
This case never sets CF.
The byte at offset 0x17 is read as bits 24-31 of the source address; the byte at offset 0x16 is not read.
The byte at offset 0x1F is read as bits 24-31 of the destination address; the byte at offset 0x1E is not read.
This case never stores AH 0x01.

INT 15h AH=88h gets the extended memory size, on a 286 or later.
CF is clear if successful.
On success AX is the number of contiguous KB starting at absolute address 100000h.
CF is set on error.
On error AH is the status.
AH=80h means invalid command (PC, PCjr).
AH=86h means function not supported (XT, PS30).
TSRs which wish to allocate extended memory to themselves often hook this call and return a reduced memory size, then using the memory between the new and old sizes.
The standard BIOS only returns memory between 1MB and 16MB.
AH=C7h is to be used for memory beyond 16MB.
Not all BIOSes return the carry flag correctly, so the call is unreliable unless support is first checked by another mechanism.
Windows 3.0 has problems when this function reports more than 15 MB, and some releases of HIMEM.SYS are limited to 15 MB for that reason.
The INT 15h handler reaches it by the case 0x88 of its main dispatch.
AX is size_extended, read from CMOS registers 0x30 and 0x31 as a 16-bit count; the case's comment says the value is capped at 64MB, not 16MB.
AX is 0 while other_memsystems is non-zero, which BIOS_ZeroExtendedSize raises and lowers.
This case never sets CF.

BL is the interrupt number of IRQ0; IRQ1-7 use the next 7 interrupts.
BH is the interrupt number of IRQ8; IRQ9-F use the next 7 interrupts.
ES:SI points to the GDT for protected mode (see #00500).

On success the CPU is in protected mode.
Execution continues with the address following the interrupt call.
BP may be destroyed.
On success all segment registers change.
BL and BH must be multiples of 8.
The protected-mode CS must reference the same memory as the CS the function is called from.

Offset 08h of the table is the GDT descriptor (see #00501).
Offset 10h of the table is the IDT descriptor.
Offset 18h of the table is the DS descriptor.
Offset 20h of the table is the ES descriptor.
Offset 28h of the table is the SS descriptor.
Offset 30h of the table is the CS descriptor.
Offset 38h of the table is uninitialized, used to build the descriptor for the BIOS CS.
The INT 15h handler reaches it by the case 0x89 of its main dispatch.
BL is written to port 0xA1 and BH to port 0x21, after a 0x10 written to port 0xA0 and port 0x20 respectively.
BH is written to port 0x21 and BL to port 0xA1, after a 0x10 written to port 0x20 and port 0xA0 respectively.
DS, ES and SS are set to selectors 0x18, 0x20 and 0x28 and CS by CPU_JMP to selector 0x30; FS and GS are not stored here.

INT 15h AH=90h is the OS hook for device busy, on the AT and PS.
AL is the device type (see #00507).
ES:BX points to the request block for type codes 80h through BFh.

Type codes 00-7F are non-reentrant devices, for which the OS must arbitrate access.
Type codes 80-BF are reentrant devices, and ES:BX points to a unique control block.
Type codes C0-FF are wait-only calls, with no complementary INT 15/AH=91h call.
Floppy and hard disk BIOS code uses this call to implement a timeout; for device types 00h and 01h, CF set means the timeout expired before the disk responded.
A multitasker should hook this function to let other tasks execute while the BIOS waits for I/O completion.
The default handler merely returns with AH=00h and CF clear.
Device types: 00h disk, 01h diskette, 02h keyboard, 03h PS/2 pointing device.
Device types: 21h waiting for keyboard input (Phoenix BIOS), 80h network, FBh digital sound (Tandy).

BH is the new state: 00h means disabled.
BH is the new state: 01h means enabled.

CF is set on error.
On error AH is the status (see #00522).
CF is clear if successful.
BH is the device ID.
BL is the value returned by the attached device after reset, AAh if the device is a mouse.
After a successful reset the pointing device is disabled, at 100 Hz sample rate, 4 counts/mm resolution, 1:1 scaling, with unchanged data package size.
This function should be called before rebooting the system (see INT 15/AH=4Fh), since otherwise the mouse may behave erratically on some systems after the boot.
Before calling this function the caller should check that the INT 15h vector is initialized; on some very old machines the IVT may contain 0000h:0000h.
IBM classifies this function as required.

INT 15h AX=C206h runs extended commands of the pointing device, on the PS/2.
BH=00h returns the device status.
With BH=00h, BL is the pointing device status (see #00524).
With BH=00h, CL is the resolution (see #00523).
With BH=00h, DL is the sample rate, in reports per second.
BH=01h sets scaling at 1:1.
BH=02h sets scaling at 2:1.

On error AH is the status (see #00522).
In the status, bit 0 is right button pressed and bit 2 is left button pressed; bits 1 and 3 are reserved.
In the status, bit 4 is 0 for 1:1 scaling and 1 for 2:1 scaling; bit 5 is device enabled.
In the status, bit 6 is 0 for stream mode and 1 for remote mode; bit 7 is reserved.
The INT 15h handler reaches it by the case 0xc2, then by case 0x06 of the dispatch on AL when en_bios_ps2mouse is set.
Bit 0 is ps2mouse.l, bit 1 is ps2mouse.r and bit 2 is ps2mouse.m, the stored mouse button states.
The status bits for reporting, mode and scaling come from ps2mouse.reporting, .mode and .scale21, which AUX commands and AUX_Reset store; AUX_Reset also clears the button states.
The resolution and sample rate returned are ps2mouse.resolution and .samplerate, which the AUX set-resolution and set-rate commands store from the byte written (resolution masked to two bits).
The status path also calls KEYBOARD_AUX_LowerIRQ and KEYBOARD_ClrBuffer, and the scaling path ends with CF clear and AH 0x00.
INT 15h AX=C207h sets the device handler address of the pointing device, on the PS/2.
ES:BX points to the FAR user device handler, or is 0000h:0000h to cancel.

When called, the handler finds on the stack: status (see #00525), X data (high byte 00h), Y data (high byte 00h) and 0000h.
The handler should return with a FAR return without popping the stack.
In the status word, bits 15-8 are reserved (0); bit 7 is Y data overflowed, bit 6 X data overflowed, bit 5 Y negative, bit 4 X negative.
In the status word, bit 3 is reserved (1), bit 2 reserved (0), bit 1 right button pressed, bit 0 left button pressed.
The INT 15h handler reaches it by the case 0xc2, then by case 0x07 of the dispatch on AL when en_bios_ps2mouse is set.
This case passes ES and BX to Mouse_ChangePS2Callback; the PS/2 callback code of mouse.cpp later jumps to the stored address.

When en_bios_ps2mouse is not set the case stores AH 0x86 and sets CF, and also clears ZF on an EGA/VGA or CGA machine.
An AL no case takes logs an unknown-call message, sets CF and stores AH 0x01.

rows.text: INT 15h AX=5300h is the APM installation check, from APM v1.0.
BX is the device ID of the system BIOS (0000h).
CF is clear if successful.
On success AH is the major version (BCD).

APM device IDs: 0000h the system BIOS, 0001h all power-managed devices, 01xxh display (01FFh all), 02xxh secondary storage (02FFh all), 03xxh parallel ports (03FFh all), 04xxh serial ports (04FFh all).

With APM v1.1 the IDs continue: 05xxh network adapters (05FFh all), 06xxh PCMCIA sockets (06FFh all), 0700h-7FFFh reserved, 80xxh system battery devices (APM v1.2), 8100h-DFFFh and F000h-FFFFh reserved, Exxxh OEM-defined.
APM system state IDs: 0000h ready (not supported for device ID 0001h), 0001h stand-by, 0002h suspend, 0003h off (not supported for 0001h in APM v1.0).
APM v1.1 adds state 0004h, the last request processing notification, and 0005h, the last request rejected, both only for device ID 0001h.
The remaining state IDs: 0006h-001Fh reserved system states, 0020h-003Fh OEM system states, 0040h-007Fh OEM device states, 0080h-FFFFh reserved device states.
AX=5307h with CX=0001h and BX=0001h puts the whole system into stand-by and returns CF clear.
Stand-by is normally entered on a stand-by request after the necessary processing, may be entered at the caller's discretion, and is typically exited on an interrupt.
AX=5307h with CX=0002h and BX=0001h suspends the system and returns CF clear after the system is resumed.
Suspend is normally entered on a suspend request after the necessary processing, and may also be entered at the caller's discretion.
It should not be called from within a hardware interrupt handler, and the caller may need to update its date and time because the suspension could be long.
AX=5307h with CX=0003h and BX=0001h (APM v1.2) turns off the system power and returns CF clear after the system is resumed.

INT 15h AX=E801h gets the memory size for configurations above 64M, from Phoenix BIOS v4.0.
CF is clear if successful.
AX is the extended memory between 1M and 16M, in K, at most 3C00h (15MB).
BX is the extended memory above 16M, in 64K blocks.
CX is the configured memory from 1M to 16M, in K.
DX is the configured memory above 16M, in 64K blocks.
CF is set on error.
It is supported by the A03 level and later XPS P90 BIOSes, the Compaq Contura, DESKPRO/i and LTE Lite 386 ROM BIOS, and AMI BIOSes dated 8/23/94 or later.
On some systems the BIOS returns AX=BX=0000h, and the caller then uses CX and DX instead.
Windows NT 3.1 and OS/2 v2.11/2.20 use this interface, and newer versions fall back to it when AX=E820h is not supported.
MS-DOS 6.0 HIMEM.SYS does not use it on an EISA machine, without a detected Compaq machine, or with the /NOABOVE16 parameter.
The INT 15h handler reaches it by the case 0xE8, then by case 0x01 of the dispatch on AL.
The case also stores CX with the same value, and caps the size at 3C00h and the block count at 65535.
This case never sets CF.
INT 15h AX=E820h gets the system memory map, from newer BIOSes.
EAX is 0000E820h on entry.
EDX is 534D4150h ("SMAP").
EBX is the continuation value, or 00000000h to start at the beginning of the map.
ECX is the size of the buffer for the result, in bytes, and should be at least 20.
ES:DI points to the buffer for the result (see #00581).
CF is clear if successful.
On success EAX is 534D4150h ("SMAP").
The buffer at ES:DI is filled.
EBX is the next offset from which to copy, or 00000000h when the list is done.
ECX is the actual length returned, in bytes.
CF is set on error.
On error AH is the error code (86h) (see #00496 at INT 15/AH=80h).
The function came with the Phoenix BIOS v4.0 and is now supported by most newer BIOSes, because Windows uses it to learn the system memory.
At most 20 bytes are transferred at a time, and some BIOSes ignore ECX on entry and always copy 20 bytes.
Some BIOSes expect the high word of EAX to be clear on entry.
When the function is unsupported, an application should fall back to AX=E802h, AX=E801h and then AH=88h.
The BIOS may return a nonzero continuation value and signal the end of the list with CF set on the next call.
The map reports base memory and contiguous ISA/PCI memory as normal, marks unused chipset holes and memory-mapped devices, marks the system BIOS reserved, and omits standard PC ranges.
A descriptor holds a QWORD base address, a QWORD length in bytes and a DWORD range type (see #00581).
Range types: 01h available memory, 02h reserved, 03h ACPI reclaim memory, 04h ACPI NVS memory, other values undefined and treated as reserved.
The INT 15h handler reaches it by the case 0xE8, then by case 0x20 of the dispatch on AL.
This case never reads EAX.
The success paths never clear CF; only the two error paths set it.

A call whose signature check fails stores EAX 0x8600 and sets CF.

A buffer size below 20 is refused with EAX 0x8600 and CF set.
The signature or size error stores EAX 0x8600, but an exhausted list stores EAX 0x534D4150 with CF set, so AH is 0x86 on one path and 0x53 on the other.

AL selects the function whose address to retrieve: 00h the read-font function, 01h the write-font function.

BH is the character size: 00h single-byte, 01h double-byte.
DH is the width of the character cell.
DL is the height of the character cell.
BP is the code page (see #00470).
CF is clear if successful.
On success AH is 00h.
ES:BX points to the requested function's address.
CF is set on error.
On error AH is the error code (see #00471).
DOS/V code pages: 0 default, 437 US English, 932 Japanese, 934 Korea, 936 China, 938 Taiwan.
DOS/V error codes: 01h invalid font type in BH, 02h BL not zero, 03h invalid font size, 04h invalid code page, 80h unsupported function (PC), 86h unsupported function (XT).
The INT 15h handler reaches it by the case 0x50 of its dispatch on AH.
The case only compares BP with 0 and never reads a code page.
The case stores AH 0x06 or 0x86; it never stores 0x01 to 0x04 or 0x80.
Writing is supported only for the 16x16 and 24x24 sizes; another size stores AH 0x06 and sets CF.
Without DOS/V the case stores AH 0x86 and sets CF.
INT 15h AX=4900h gets the BIOS type of a Far East MS-DOS system.
CF is clear if successful.
On success AH is 00h.
BL is the BIOS mode: 00h DOS/V, 01h standard DBCS DOS with hardware DBCS support.
CF is set on error.
On error AH is 86h, function not supported.
In practice DOS/J returns AH=86h, and AX DOS does not support this call.
The INT 15h handler reaches it by the case 0x49 of its dispatch on AH.
The case stores BL 0 and never the DOS/V or DBCS mode distinction, because it always answers DOS/V when the machine is one.
